$meta.title: F18A enhanced VDP registers
$meta.description: Hand-authored from upstream sources, because there is no local source of truth for this one: the ACE's video card is a Pico9918, and its F18A personality is defined by Matthew Hagerty's F18A HDL and by the Pico9918 firmware, neither of which lives in this ecosystem. Unlike every other file in this directory it therefore cannot be regenerated, and unlike every other file in this directory almost none of it can be checked by running it — the emulator is a stock TMS9918A and masks register writes to 0-7. What can be checked is checked: the detection samples run in CI and assert the stock-VDP path.

sources.title: F18A register-use spreadsheet, sheets V1.9 and V1.8
sources.author: Matthew Hagerty
sources.authority: The shipped F18A register map. Where anything disagrees with the F18A forum documentation, this wins — the forum posts were written during development and several registers moved afterwards.

sources.title: F18A documentation (collected forum posts)
sources.author: Matthew Hagerty
sources.authority: The only narrative explanation of why the parts work the way they do — unlocking, the bitplane scheme, the paging model, the PIX instruction. Its register numbers are dev-era and several are stale; its explanations are not.

sources.title: Pico9918 F18A Programmer's Reference wiki
sources.author: Troy Schrapel
sources.authority: The authority for an ACE, because an ACE has a Pico9918 and not an F18A. Adds registers the F18A never had and drops hardware the F18A had.

$meta.bitNumbering: D7 is the most significant bit, matching the rest of this site and the Pico9918 reference. Hagerty's own documents number bits the other way round, so his tables read mirrored against these.
$meta.unresolved: Claims the three sources disagree about are carried in the `conflict` field of whatever they belong to, and recorded in ACCURACY.md. None of them is silently resolved.

port.note: The same two addresses the stock card uses. Everything below is reached through them.

unlock.summary: Write $1C to register 57, twice, with no other card access in between.
unlock.why: Register 57 is register 1 on a stock TMS9918A, which only looks at the low three bits of a register number. $1C written to register 1 means 4 KB of VRAM, display blanked, interrupts off, both mode bits set at once — an illegal combination that makes the chip useless. No working program would write it once, let alone twice in a row.
unlock.hazard: On a stock card those two writes land in register 1 and blank the screen. Set register 1 back to something sane immediately afterwards, whether or not the unlock took.
unlock.cancels: Any other register write between the two cancels the sequence.
relock: Write a value with bit 7 set to register 50. Registers return to power-on defaults and the palette survives.
Write $C0 to register 50 to reset the palette as well (Pico9918).

values.means: an F18A personality running on something else — on an ACE, the Pico9918

identity.note: Bits 7-5 are the identity field; 111 is the F18A. Bit 3 is the emulation marker. Reading status register 1 needs the card unlocked first, because register 15 is an enhanced register.

gpuProbe.summary: The test everyone uses. Six bytes of TMS9900 machine code that erase their own first instruction.
gpuProbe.result: $3F00 reads back $00 if a GPU ran the code, and $04 — the top byte of the CLR opcode, untouched — if nothing did.
gpuProbe.hazard: Registers 54 and 55 are registers 6 and 7 on a stock card, so a failed probe leaves the sprite pattern table address and the screen colors wrong. Put them back.

registers.name: Mode control 1
registers.summary: Mode bits, plus the horizontal interrupt enable.

bits.name: IE1
bits.description: Horizontal interrupt enable — pairs with register 19

registers.name: Mode control 2
registers.summary: VRAM size, display enable, vertical interrupt, mode bits, sprite size.

registers.name: Name table base address
registers.summary: Tile layer 1 name table, on a 1 KB boundary. Address = (VR2 & $0F) << 10.
notes: 768 bytes per page at 24 rows, 960 bytes at 30 rows.
When paged scrolling is on, the extra pages are found by flipping bits in this address rather than by another register.

registers.name: Color table base address
registers.summary: On a 64-byte boundary. Becomes the tile attribute table in the enhanced color modes.
notes: 32 bytes in the original color mode.
256 bytes as a tile attribute table, one entry per pattern.
768 bytes to 4 KB in position-attribute mode, depending on page sizes.

registers.name: Pattern generator base address
registers.summary: On a 2 KB boundary. Shared by both tile layers.
notes: 2 KB for 256 patterns in the original color mode.
4 KB in 2-bit color, 6 KB in 3-bit color — the extra bitplanes follow the first.

registers.name: Sprite attribute table base address
registers.summary: On a 128-byte boundary. 32 sprites, four bytes each.

registers.name: Sprite pattern generator base address
registers.summary: On a 2 KB boundary. 4 KB in 2-bit color, 6 KB in 3-bit color.

registers.name: Foreground / background color
registers.summary: Text color in the high nibble, backdrop in the low nibble.

registers.name: Name table 2 base address
registers.summary: Tile layer 2's name table, same format as register 2.
registers.conflict: The forum documentation gives this register to a "fixed map" — a bitmap saying which tiles scroll — and describes it as 7 bits on a 128-byte boundary. The fixed map did not ship; the register became tile layer 2's name table.

registers.name: Color table 2 base address
registers.summary: Tile layer 2's color / attribute table, same format and same rules as register 3.

registers.name: Status register select and counter control
registers.summary: Picks which of the sixteen status registers the status port returns, and drives the on-card timer.

bits.name: CNT_SNAP
bits.description: Latch the counter so it can be read, without stopping it

bits.name: SR_SEL
bits.description: Status register 0-15 the next status read returns

notes: Selecting 0 gives the stock status byte, with the usual side effects: the interrupt flag clears, the collision and fifth-sprite bits reset, and palette write mode ends.

Selecting anything else returns that register with none of those side effects — which is also the trap. Leave the selection pointing somewhere else and the machine's own interrupt handler reads the wrong byte and never acknowledges the interrupt.

registers.name: Horizontal interrupt scan line
registers.summary: Raise an interrupt when the beam reaches this line. 0 disables it.
notes: Register 0's IE1 bit must be set as well.
There is only one interrupt line, so a handler has to work out which of the two fired by reading status register 1.

registers.name: Palette select
registers.summary: Which 16-color block of the 64 palette registers each layer draws from, in the lower color modes.
notes: The selected value is shifted up four bits and combined with the color index to make the six-bit palette address.
Unused for tiles and sprites in 2-bit color, where the pattern supplies those bits instead.

registers.name: Tile layer 2 horizontal scroll
registers.summary: Whole tiles in the high five bits, pixels within a tile in the low three.

registers.name: Tile layer 2 vertical scroll
registers.summary: 0-255 pixels, added straight to the Y position. Past the bottom of the display it wraps, or swaps page if vertical paging is on.

registers.name: Tile layer 1 horizontal scroll
registers.summary: Same format as register 25, for the main tile layer.

registers.name: Tile layer 1 vertical scroll
registers.summary: Same as register 26, for the main tile layer.

registers.name: Page sizes and pattern plane spacing
registers.summary: How wide and tall each tile layer's virtual screen is, and how far apart the extra color bitplanes sit.

bits.name: SPGS
bits.description: Sprite pattern plane spacing — 00 = 2 KB, 01 = 1 KB, 10 = 512 B, 11 = 256 B

bits.name: HPSIZE2
bits.description: Tile layer 2 horizontal pages — 0 = one, 1 = two (64 tiles wide)

bits.name: TPGS
bits.description: Tile pattern plane spacing, same encoding as SPGS

notes: Plane spacing is 0x800 >> the two-bit value.
The page-size bits are what turn a scroll register from wrapping in place into scrolling onto new ground.
registers.conflict: The forum documentation puts the page-size bits in register 30 alongside a horizontal banner size, and uses register 29 for page-start bits. Neither arrangement shipped.

registers.name: Maximum sprites per scan line
registers.summary: How many sprites the card will draw on one line before it gives up. The stock chip's answer is four.
notes: The Pico9918 defaults to 31. Writing 0 restores that default.
On a real F18A, writing 0 restores whatever the card's jumper says.

registers.name: Bitmap layer control
registers.summary: The whole of the bitmap layer's behavior in one byte.

bits.name: BML_PRI
bits.description: 0 = below the tile layers, 1 = above them

bits.name: BML_FAT
bits.description: 0 = 1×1 pixels, four colors; 1 = 2×1 pixels, sixteen colors

bits.name: BML_PAL
bits.description: Palette select — shifted up two bits and combined with the pixel value

registers.conflict: The v1.8 sheet calls D6 priority over sprites, the v1.9 sheet calls it priority over tiles. The v1.9 reading is the one the layer-priority rules bear out: the bitmap layer is never drawn above a sprite.

registers.name: Bitmap layer base address
registers.summary: Where the bitmap lives in VRAM. Address = VR32 << 6, so a 64-byte boundary.

registers.name: Bitmap layer X position
registers.summary: 0-255. The bitmap moves independently of everything else, and scroll registers do not touch it.

registers.name: Bitmap layer Y position
registers.summary: The first scan line the bitmap is drawn on. Nothing above it.

registers.name: Bitmap layer width
registers.summary: Width of one bitmap row, in bytes. Every byte is four pixels wide whichever pixel format is selected.
registers.conflict: The Pico9918 reference states the encoding as "0 = 64 bytes, otherwise VR35 >> 2". Hagerty's sheets call the register plain "bitmap width". Untested here either way.

registers.name: Bitmap layer height
registers.summary: How many rows are drawn, starting from the row in register 34.

registers.name: Palette control and data-port mode
registers.summary: Points the data port at palette memory instead of VRAM, and says which entry.

bits.name: DPM
bits.description: Data port mode — 0 = writes go to VRAM, 1 = writes go to the palette

bits.name: AUTO
bits.description: Step to the next palette entry after each complete entry

notes: One entry is two writes to the data port.
Without auto-increment, palette mode ends by itself after those two writes.
With auto-increment it stays on until you clear it, or until the index rolls over past 63, or until any status register is read.

registers.name: VRAM address increment
registers.summary: Signed byte added to the VRAM address after every read or write. Default 1.
notes: $FF steps backwards. 0 holds the address still. 2 and up skip — one write per pixel row, say, instead of one per byte.

registers.name: Enhanced color modes and display options
registers.summary: Turns on tile layer 2, 30-row mode, and the enhanced color modes for tiles and sprites separately.

bits.name: ECMT
bits.description: Tile color mode — 0 = original, 1 / 2 / 3 = one, two or three bits per pixel

bits.name: Y_REAL
bits.description: Sprite Y is the real coordinate rather than the stock chip's off-by-one

bits.name: ECMS
bits.description: Sprite color mode, same encoding as ECMT

notes: D2 was a sprite-linking enable in v1.8, letting a sprite follow a parent sprite. It was dropped for v1.9 and is not in the Pico9918.

registers.name: General control and GPU triggers
registers.summary: The odds and ends: reset, GPU triggers, layer disable, sprite reporting, scan lines, attribute mode, layer priority.

bits.name: VR_RST
bits.description: Reset — relocks the card and restores register defaults; the palette survives

bits.name: GPU_HTRIG
bits.description: Run the GPU at the start of every scan line

bits.name: GPU_VTRIG
bits.description: Run the GPU once per frame

bits.name: TL1_OFF
bits.description: Turn off tile layer 1 — sprites, the bitmap layer and tile layer 2 carry on

bits.name: RPT_MAX
bits.description: 0 = report the fifth sprite the stock way, 1 = report against register 30's limit

bits.name: SCANLINES
bits.description: Dim every other line for a CRT look

bits.name: POS_ATTR
bits.description: 0 = attributes per pattern name, 1 = attributes per screen position

bits.name: T2_PRI
bits.description: 0 = tile layer 2 always on top, 1 = tile layer 2 obeys per-tile priority

notes: Writing $C0 resets the palette as well (Pico9918).
registers.conflict: The forum documentation uses registers 50-53 as scroll-limit registers defining a window that scrolling cannot leave. That design did not ship in this form.

registers.name: Maximum sprites per frame
registers.summary: The highest sprite the card will process at all, 0-32. Default 32.
notes: Independent of register 30, which is a per-line limit.
It is also the only way to stop sprite processing early in 30-row mode, where the $D0 terminator is a legal Y coordinate.

registers.name: GPU program counter, high byte
registers.summary: Default $40, which points at the GPU's own RAM.

registers.name: GPU program counter, low byte
registers.summary: Writing this loads the program counter and starts the GPU running. It is the trigger, not just the low byte.

registers.name: GPU control and status
registers.summary: Write 0 to load the program counter without running; write 1 to start. Reading it says whether the GPU is running.

bits.name: GPU OP
bits.description: Write: 0 = reset and load the PC, 1 = run. Read: 1 = running

registers.name: Unlock
registers.summary: Write $1C twice in a row to unlock. Any write to it once unlocked locks it again.

registers.name: Configuration option index
registers.summary: Selects a card configuration option. Writing it also mirrors that option's current value into status register 12.
notes: On a real F18A v1.8 this register was a GROM clock divider, which has nothing to do with the Pico9918's use of it.

registers.name: Configuration option value
registers.summary: Writes the option selected by register 58. Options below index 8 are read-only hardware facts and refuse writes.

registers.name: Firmware update control
registers.summary: How the card's own configuration tool updates its firmware through the video port.
notes: Reads one 512-byte frame at a time, and refuses to run while the GPU is running.

statusRegisters.name: Standard status
statusRegisters.summary: The stock TMS9918A status byte, and the only one a locked card will give you.

bits.name: INT
bits.description: Vertical interrupt — cleared by this read

bits.name: 5S
bits.description: Too many sprites on a line

notes: Reading it clears the interrupt flag, resets the collision and fifth-sprite bits, and ends palette write mode.

statusRegisters.name: Identity and horizontal interrupt
statusRegisters.summary: What the card is, and whether the horizontal interrupt fired.

bits.name: EMU
bits.description: 1 = an F18A personality rather than F18A silicon

bits.name: BLANK
bits.description: In a blanking period right now

bits.name: HF
bits.description: Horizontal interrupt fired — stays set until this register is read

statusRegisters.name: GPU status
statusRegisters.summary: D7 is set while the GPU is running. D6-D0 are seven bits the GPU program can set for the 6502 to read.

statusRegisters.name: Current scan line
statusRegisters.summary: Where the beam is. 0 outside the active display.

statusRegisters.name: Nanosecond counter, high
statusRegisters.summary: The top two bits of the nanosecond count.

statusRegisters.name: Second counter, high
statusRegisters.summary: The high byte of the second count.

statusRegisters.name: Configuration mirror
statusRegisters.summary: The value of whichever option register 58 last selected.

statusRegisters.name: Temperature
statusRegisters.summary: The Pico's core temperature, four counts per degree C. Updated every 64 frames.

statusRegisters.name: Version
statusRegisters.summary: Major and minor version, a nibble each. An ACE reads $1A.

statusRegisters.name: Select mirror
statusRegisters.summary: Reads back the status register selection written to register 15.

colorModes.description: The stock chip. Pattern bits say where the ink goes, and the color comes from somewhere else entirely.
Pattern bits become color indexes. Same one plane, but every tile picks its own pair out of 64 colors.
A second plane 2 KB along. Four colors in every 8×8 tile and every sprite.
A third plane. Eight colors per tile, per sprite, with no cell-color rule anywhere in sight.

colorModeNote: Sprite color 0 is always transparent, so a sprite shows one fewer color than a tile in the same mode. Tiles choose, per tile, whether index 0 is transparent or a real color.
colorModeConflict: The Pico9918 reference tabulates these one step higher — 4, 8 and 16 colors from 2, 3 and 4 bitplanes. The F18A's own HDL, its register sheets and its author's worked examples all give 2, 4 and 8 from 1, 2 and 3 planes, and the pattern-table sizes only add up that way. The lower set is what this site documents.

palette.depth: 12-bit, four bits each of red, green and blue — 4096 colors
palette.format: Two bytes per entry. One carries red in its low nibble, the other green and blue in its two nibbles.
palette.picoFormat: The Pico9918 puts an alpha nibble in the spare four bits, and documents $F there as fully opaque.
palette.writeOrderConflict: Hagerty's worked example sends the red byte first and the green-blue byte second. The Pico9918 reference describes the opposite order. Both cannot be right and neither can be checked here — write four entries, look at the screen, and believe your eyes.
palette.survivesReset: Palette changes outlive a soft reset. Only a power cycle, or an explicit palette reset, puts the default colors back.

defaults.name: The same sixteen, arranged for 1-bit color
defaults.description: Every even entry black, every odd entry one of the stock colors, so a two-color tile is one color on black without touching the palette.

defaults.name: CGA arranged for 1-bit color
defaults.description: The same trick as palette 1, over the CGA colors.

bits.name: EC
bits.description: Early clock — shift the sprite 32 pixels left

spriteUnlocked.title: Sprite attribute byte, card unlocked

bits.name: SIZE
bits.description: Per-sprite size — 0 takes register 1's global setting, 1 forces 16×16

bits.name: PS
bits.description: Color, or palette select in the enhanced color modes

spriteUnlocked.conflict: The Pico9918 reference calls D4 an opaque-sprite flag in 16×16 mode rather than a size override. Both documents agree the bit is new and that it concerns 16×16 sprites; they do not agree on what it does.

tile.title: Tile attribute byte, enhanced color modes
tile.note: In the enhanced color modes the color table stops being a color table. Each entry becomes an attribute byte for one pattern — or for one screen position, with position attributes on.

bits.name: TRANS
bits.description: Color index 0 is transparent rather than a color

textPosition.title: Attribute byte in 40- and 80-column text, position attributes on

priority.summary: Priority is worked out per pixel, not per layer, so one tile layer can be both in front of and behind the same sprite on one line.
stages: Tile layer 2 replaces it wherever layer 2 is not transparent.
That pixel carries a priority flag if the tile's PRI bit is set, or if it came from layer 2 while T2_PRI is clear.
The bitmap layer replaces it where the bitmap is enabled, in range and not transparent, and either has priority or the tile pixel was transparent. A bitmap pixel clears the priority flag.
A sprite wins unless the surviving pixel has priority.
rules: The bitmap layer is never drawn over a sprite. Its priority bit positions it against tiles only.
A transparent pixel has no priority to assert, so everything below shows through regardless of the PRI bit.
T2_PRI is backwards from what its name suggests: clear it and layer 2 sits above sprites unconditionally.
Between sprites nothing has changed — the lowest-numbered sprite still wins.

paging.summary: Each name table page is 1 KB. Extra pages are found by flipping address bits, not by another base register.

bits.effect: A second page 1 KB above the first — a virtual screen 64 tiles wide
A second page 2 KB above the first — seamless wrap top to bottom

layouts.behavior: Scrolls sideways onto page 1; wraps vertically
Scrolls vertically onto page 1; wraps sideways
A 64 × 48 tile field, no wrapping at all

paging.colorTable: The color table follows the name table's page bits by itself. Set its base once and leave it alone.
paging.patternTable: One pattern table serves every page, and both tile layers.
paging.note: In 30-row mode a page is 960 bytes rather than 768, so only 64 bytes go spare between pages instead of 256 — which is why pages sit on 1 KB boundaries at all.

gpu.summary: A TMS9900 inside the video card, with its own RAM, direct access to VRAM, the palette and every VDP register, and a pixel-plotting instruction the 9900 never had.

memoryMap.what: VRAM — the same 16 KB the 6502 reaches through the data port
GRAM — the GPU's own RAM, where its code normally lives
Palette RAM, 64 entries of two bytes, word access only
The VDP registers, readable and writable

gpu.picoMemoryNote: A real F18A leaves everything outside its defined regions unimplemented. The Pico9918 backs the whole 64 KB with RAM, so roughly 40 KB of scratch space exists that F18A code cannot assume.

f18aOnlyMemory.what: A 32-bit free-running counter on the F18A. On the Pico9918 this address is the DMA trigger instead.

newInstructions.name: CALL
newInstructions.what: Call a subroutine, pushing the return address

changedInstructions.name: XOP
changedInstructions.what: Plot, read, test or address a pixel in one instruction

changedInstructions.name: IDLE
changedInstructions.what: Stop until the next trigger. Safe here, unlike on a real 9900 in a computer

changedInstructions.name: RTWP
changedInstructions.what: R14 to the program counter, R15 to the flags. R13 is not used

changedInstructions.name: CKON
changedInstructions.what: F18A only — chip select low on its flash chip

changedInstructions.name: LDCR
changedInstructions.what: F18A only — write a byte to flash

changedInstructions.name: STCR
changedInstructions.what: F18A only — read a byte from flash

gpu.unimplementedWhy: There is no workspace pointer, no interrupt system and no CRU, so the instructions that use them are gone. An unknown opcode does nothing at all rather than derailing the GPU.
gpu.stack: R15 is the stack pointer. Set it before the first CALL or PUSH — $47FE, the top of GPU RAM, is the conventional value. The stack grows down and is always words on even addresses.

pix.summary: One instruction that reads, writes, conditionally writes, or merely locates a pixel, given X and Y.
pix.sourceOperand: X and Y as two bytes, X in the high byte, both 0-255. Any addressing mode.

fields.what: 1 = work out a Graphics II address instead of a bitmap-layer one
1 = return the address rather than touching the pixel
1 = read the current pixel back into PP, after any write
1 = write only if the comparison in E holds
1 = write only where the pixel equals OO; 0 = only where it does not
The pixel value to compare against
The pixel value to write, and where a read comes back

pix.why: The address arithmetic it replaces is eight instructions of bit-twiddling in the TI Editor/Assembler manual. In hardware it is an adder and some wiring.

dma.summary: A block copier the Pico9918 adds, driven by a command block at $8000 and triggered by touching that address.

fields.what: D0 = hold the source address, D1 = write the destination backwards

triggers: Writing register 55 starts it once, at that address.
Register 50's GPU_HTRIG starts it at the top of every scan line.
Register 50's GPU_VTRIG starts it once per frame.
f18aOnlyFeatures: A serial flash chip the GPU can read and write, holding the FPGA bit stream, the default palettes and about 22 character sets. Writing the wrong part of it bricks the card.
A small catalog of preloaded routines in that flash: block copy, font load, and three for reading the catalog itself.
A hardware random number generator and a free-running 32-bit counter in the GPU's address space.
